blocks.text: Chapter 6.
Overconfidence: Illusions, Formulas, and the Premortem
Sixth night, friend — and it opens with a story you already know... told wrong.

Two graduate students at Stanford build a search engine. Genius founders, inevitable triumph — the legend writes itself. But here's the scene the legend leaves out: early on, Larry Page and Sergey Brin tried to sell Google — for under one million dollars — and the buyer turned them down. One shrug in a conference room, friend, and the inevitable empire almost never existed. That's Nassim Taleb's narrative fallacy: we compress the messy past into tidy stories of talent and intention, quietly deleting luck — and the better the story explains, the less we notice what it leaves out.

The past even edits your memory. Before Nixon's historic 1972 trips to China and the USSR, Baruch Fischhoff had people assign probabilities to the possible outcomes. Afterward, they misremembered their own forecasts as closer to what actually happened. "I knew it all along" isn't a boast, friend — it's a memory distortion. And hindsight breeds outcome bias: we grade decisions by results instead of by the reasoning available at the time — so the official who took wise precautions against a disaster that never came looks paranoid, while the reckless gambler who got lucky looks like a visionary. That grading system punishes prudence everywhere, from politics to medicine.

Kahneman felt the deeper illusion in his own hands. As a young army psychologist, he assessed officer candidates on a leaderless-group obstacle test — and formed vivid, certain impressions of who would lead. The feedback from officer school came back: his forecasts were barely better than blind guesses. And here's the chilling part, friend: knowing that changed nothing. The next batch of candidates produced the same vivid certainty. He named it the illusion of validity — confidence is a feeling produced by the coherence of a story, and it is utterly insensitive to evidence that the story predicts nothing.

Pause and guess: Terry Odean analyzed 10,000 individual brokerage accounts — every trade, over years. When an investor sold stock A to buy stock B, the trader was expressing a confident judgment: B will beat A. On average, what actually happened?
Ready? Here is what happened.

The shares they SOLD went on to beat the shares they BOUGHT — by about 3.2 percentage points a year, before costs, friend. Every confident swap was, on average, a small act of self-harm. The follow-up study's title says it all: "Trading Is Hazardous to Your Wealth" — the most active traders earned the worst returns, and men, who trade more, did worse than women. The professionals fare no better: year-to-year persistence in mutual-fund results is essentially zero, and when Kahneman computed the year-over-year rank correlations of advisers at a wealth firm across eight years, the average was .01 — the annual bonuses were rewarding luck — and the firm, shown its own numbers, quietly went back to business as usual. Philip Tetlock then did it to the pundits: roughly 80,000 expert political and economic forecasts — performing worse than simple base-rate rules, barely better than chance, confidence undented. The louder, single-big-idea "hedgehogs" made the worst and most-quoted predictions; the doubt-tolerant "foxes" did a little better. The rule to carry, friend: in an unpredictable world, sincere high confidence in a long-range forecast is a warning sign, not a credential — including when the forecaster is you.
The dumb little formula that wins

So if confident judgment fails, what wins? Something almost insulting, friend: simple formulas. In 1954 Paul Meehl showed that plain statistical rules built from a few scores matched or beat trained clinicians — a result now replicated in more than two hundred domains: medical prognoses, credit risk, parole outcomes, wine prices. Experts lose because they attempt clever, complex judgments — and because human judgment is noisy: shown the same case twice, an expert often disagrees with himself. A formula never does.

Economist Orley Ashenfelter predicts the quality of Bordeaux vintages from three weather numbers — summer heat, harvest rain, winter rain — with a correlation above .90, outperforming the swirling, sniffing tasters. Robyn Dawes proved you don't even need fancy statistics: equal weights on a few sensible variables do about as well as optimal regressions. And the most beautiful example saved the most lives: in 1953, anesthesiologist Virginia Apgar wrote down five observable signs of a newborn — heart rate, breathing, reflex, muscle tone, color — scored each 0 to 2, and replaced every obstetrician's varying intuition with one number. The Apgar score is still used on nearly every baby born today, friend. A checklist, beating a feeling, forever.

When can you trust a gut? Kahneman and his intellectual rival Gary Klein — champion of brilliant fireground commanders — spent years on exactly that question and converged: intuition, as Herbert Simon said, is "nothing more and nothing less than recognition" — pattern matching from memory. So it's trustworthy only when two conditions BOTH hold: the environment is regular enough to have patterns... and the judge had prolonged practice with rapid, clear feedback to learn them. Chess, firefighting, anesthesiology: yes. Stock picking and long-range punditry: the environment is close to random — experience there breeds confidence, never skill. Never rate an intuition by the confidence of its delivery, friend. Ask instead: could this person actually have learned this?

Pause and guess: Kahneman himself fell into this chapter's final trap — while writing a textbook ABOUT decision-making. His team estimated the project would take about two years. Then he asked the curriculum expert on his own team a simple outside-view question: how did OTHER teams like ours fare? What did the expert say — and what did the team do with the answer?
Ready? Here is what happened.

The expert reported, from memory of many similar teams: about 40 percent never finished at all — and none finished in under seven years. A death sentence for the two-year plan, delivered by their own colleague, from their own data. And what did they do, friend? They nodded... and kept working to the two-year plan. The book took eight years and was never used. That's the planning fallacy: the inside view — your plan, your team, your best-case simulation — feels informed and always wins the argument, while the outside view — the statistics of similar projects — is boring and right. The base rates are grim everywhere: the Scottish Parliament building, estimated at up to £40 million, finished at £431 million; Flyvbjerg's worldwide rail database shows average cost overruns above 40 percent with ridership overestimated 90 percent of the time — and no improvement in thirty years, because every new team takes the inside view; American kitchen remodels budgeted at $18,700 came in at $38,800. The cure is reference-class forecasting, now mandated for big British public projects: find the class of similar projects, take ITS distribution as your baseline, and adjust only for specific, defensible differences. And since optimism is capitalism's engine — 81 percent of founders rate their odds at 70 percent or better while only 35 percent of small businesses survive five years; Duke's CFOs gave 11,000 market forecasts whose 80-percent confidence intervals were right a third of the time — finish every big plan with Gary Klein's premortem, friend: gather the team when the decision is nearly final and announce, "It's one year from now. We implemented the plan. It was a disaster. Take ten minutes and write the history of that disaster." Doubt becomes loyal, skeptics become heroes, and the failure modes surface while you can still fix them.
Before you go

So: the past is a story that deletes luck — Google was nearly sold for pocket change; hindsight rewrites your own memories and grades decisions by outcomes; confidence is a feeling about coherence, not a measurement of truth — traders, advisers, and pundits prove it with their own records; dumb formulas beat clever experts wherever the world is noisy — score six traits and commit; trust intuition only where patterns exist and feedback taught them; and every plan deserves the outside view plus a ten-minute premortem. This week, friend: for your biggest current estimate, find one reference class — how did projects like this actually turn out? — and start your number there.

Tomorrow, the summit: the theory that won Kahneman the Nobel Prize. Why does losing a hundred dollars hurt roughly twice as much as winning a hundred feels good — and how did one insight about a reference point topple two centuries of economics? Next time: prospect theory — losses loom larger.
Key takeaways
The narrative fallacy deletes luck: Google was nearly sold for under $1M — and hindsight bias rewrites even your own past forecasts ("I knew it all along" is memory distortion).

Confidence measures story coherence, not accuracy: Odean's traders' sold shares beat their bought ones by 3.2pp/yr; adviser skill correlated .01 year to year; Tetlock's 80,000 expert forecasts lost to base rates.
Prefer the formula in noisy domains: Meehl's 200+ replications, Bordeaux from three weather numbers, the Apgar score — equal weights on six traits beat unstructured interviews.
Trust intuition only when the environment is regular AND the judge had long practice with fast, clear feedback — otherwise it's a story in the costume of expertise.
Planning fallacy: take the outside view — reference-class base rates first (Kahneman's own 2-year plan took 8; Scottish Parliament £40M→£431M), adjust only for defensible differences.
Optimism powers economies and wrecks forecasts (CFO 80% intervals right ~1/3 of the time) — so run a ten-minute premortem: "it's a year from now and this failed — write the history."
